summary: This Experimental document describes using Geo-Coordinates in LISP and defines a new LCAF encoding for them. It updates RFC 8060.

plainLanguage.summary: It adds a place on the map, latitude and longitude, to the address labels used by a routing system.

subtitle: A new LISP address format for putting latitude, longitude and an optional radius into mapping records.

tldr.problem: LISP mapping records can say where a device is in network terms, but not where it is on the map, and the older Geo-Coordinates encoding in RFC 8060 was less compact than desired.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 10040 defines the Geo-Location LCAF type (type 17), which encodes a Geo-Point (latitude, longitude, altitude) or a Geo-Prefix (a Geo-Point plus a radius) in EID-Records and RLOC-Records.
tldr.outcome: It deprecates LCAF type 5 from RFC 8060. Because location data is sensitive, the document stresses access policy, signed and encrypted Map-Replies, and short TTLs.

today: RFC 10040 is an Experimental IETF RFC published in September 2026 that updates RFC 8060; no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. IANA assigned LCAF type 17 and marked type 5 as deprecated.

sections.title: Geo-Coordinates in LISP
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP, RFC 9300) separates identity from location with two namespaces: Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) and Routing Locators (RLOCs). Both can be written in LISP control messages using a general syntax with Address Family Identifiers.

This document defines a new LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF) encoding for Geo-Coordinates. It deviates from the structure in RFC 9179 because a more compact encoding was desired. It updates RFC 8060 by deprecating the Geo-Coordinates encoding there (LCAF type 5) in favor of the new type, named Geo-Location. The new type is used in EID-Records and RLOC-Records.

The RFC says it is part of a development effort and is not part of an experiment, because not all Experimental RFCs are necessarily part of an experiment; it is about the maturity level of the technology.
sections.plainLanguage: LISP already had a way to write a location on a map, but this RFC replaces it with a smaller, tidier one.

sections.title: Geo-Points and Geo-Prefixes
sections.content: A Geo-Point is a coordinate, as defined by the WGS 84 reference the RFC cites, given as latitude, longitude and altitude. A Geo-Prefix is a sphere that covers a geographic area, made of a Geo-Point and a radius. A Geo-Point is more specific than a Geo-Prefix when its physical location lies inside the sphere.
sections.plainLanguage: A Geo-Point is a pin on the map. A Geo-Prefix is a pin with a circle drawn around it.

sections.title: Where Geo-Data Goes in Mapping Records
sections.content:
Geo-Points MAY be put in an RLOC-Record to give the physical location of an Egress Tunnel Router (ETR) or Re-encapsulating Tunneling Router (RTR), which helps when topological distance is inaccurate or hidden. Alongside RLOC addresses, the AFI-List LCAF type SHOULD be used. A Geo-Point MAY also be the only content of an RLOC-Record, so that an EID maps directly to a location. For example, a package tracking number embedded in an IPv6 EID can map to the geo-point of the LISP node that last registered it, so new registrations track the package as it moves.

A Geo-Prefix in an RLOC-Record gives a coarse location, such as a city or country. A Geo-Prefix can also be an EID-Prefix. When a Geo-Point is used as the lookup key, a sort of longest match applies: a matching entry MUST be returned, and if several Geo-Prefixes match, all of them MUST be returned, using the overlapping lookup semantics of RFC 9301.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone book entry can say exactly where someone is, or only roughly, like 'somewhere in this city'. Asking about a spot returns every rough area that covers it.

sections.title: Worked Uses
sections.content:
The RFC combines mappings to answer 'Is the package in San Francisco?' with two lookups. The first returns the package's geo-point; the second looks up that geo-point and, if it is inside a 60-mile radius Geo-Prefix registered for San Francisco, returns that mapping. If the package is not in San Francisco, the second lookup fails.

Two other uses are described. In Wi-Fi coverage, rings of access points can be modeled as concentric spheres, helping choose a better access point and the right moment to move between Wi-Fi access points or 3GPP base stations. In vehicular networks, a Geo-Prefix can form a reachability set of Roadside Units, so an Ingress Tunnel Router can encapsulate to several RLOCs while the vehicle roams.
sections.plainLanguage: If you drop a pin for a parcel and a big circle for a city, you can ask whether the pin sits inside the circle.

sections.title: The Geo-Location LCAF Encoding
sections.content:
The encoding uses AFI 16387 (the LCAF format) and LCAF Type 17. Without VPNs it is used alone in an EID-Record; with VPNs it is encoded in the AFI field of the Instance-ID LCAF type. The document has no provision to validate the location values.

Flag bits control the meaning: U (location uncertainty in use), N (latitude north of the Equator when set, south when clear), E (longitude east of the Prime Meridian when set, west when clear), A (altitude in use), M (altitude in meters when set, centimeters when clear), R (radius in use, so it is a Geo-Prefix; otherwise a Geo-Point) and K (radius in kilometers when set, meters when clear). Latitude degrees range 0 to 90 and longitude degrees 0 to 180, each with a 24-bit milliseconds part up to 3,599,999. Altitude is a signed 32-bit number, and the radius is an unsigned 16-bit number.

For compatibility, EID-Records with this type work only on LISP nodes that support them. An RLOC-Record with the type that reaches a node that does not understand it is ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The record is a small form: tick boxes say north or south, east or west, and whether the radius is in meters or kilometers, then come the numbers.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Registering Geo-Coordinates makes an xTR's physical location known to queriers and to the Mapping Database System. A policy on who may see it is typically kept on the xTR and applied when the Mapping Service Provider forwards Map-Requests. The xTR can answer with all RLOC-Records or leave out those with Geo-Coordinates. If the provider proxies Map-Replies, it MUST apply the xTR policy so only authorized requesters see the data. Map-Replies are signed as in RFC 9303 and can be encrypted.

Tracking of hosts can occur if a Geo-Coordinate-encoded RLOC is associated with an EID assigned to a host. The privacy section suggests using signatures to authorize requesters, using Geo-Prefixes to obfuscate a Geo-Point, and using short TTLs. It adds that typical use is the location of well-known public structures, places and landmarks rather than people, vehicles and equipment.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling everyone exactly where something is can be risky, so the owner decides who may ask, and can share only a rough circle.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in bytes after the Length field.

fields.name: U N E A M R K
fields.desc: Flag bits for uncertainty, hemispheres, altitude and radius units.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: MUST be set to 0 when sending and ignored when receiving.

fields.name: Altitude
fields.desc: Signed; meters or centimeters relative to sea level.

fields.name: Radius
fields.desc: Radius of the sphere when the R-bit is set.

fields.name: AFI
fields.desc: Address family of the Address field.
